title: Binary Search Tree (BST)
description: BST ordering invariant, unique keys, height convention, three deletion cases with in-order successor, four tree traversals, and balanced vs. skewed complexity on bst.html.

questions.prompt: A binary tree has root 50. Its left child is 30, and 30's right child is 55. Is this a valid Binary Search Tree?
choices: No: 55 is in the left subtree of 50, so it must be strictly smaller than 50
Yes: 55 is greater than its parent 30, which is all a BST requires
Yes: 55 only needs to be smaller than the maximum key in the tree
No: a left child is not allowed to have a right child
questions.answer: No: 55 is in the left subtree of 50, so it must be strictly smaller than 50
questions.explanation: The BST ordering invariant applies across every ancestor, not just the immediate parent: every key in 50's entire left subtree must be strictly less than 50, so 55 violates the bound (a search for 55 from 50 would go right and never find it). Saying yes because 55 > 30 is the classic mistake of checking only parent-child pairs.
questions.page: On bst.html: try inserting 50, 30, then 55 and notice 55 goes to the right of 50, never under 30.

questions.prompt: In this BST visualizer, an empty tree has height -1 and a single-node tree has height 0.
questions.explanation: This visualizer uses the edge-count height convention: height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single root node has 0 edges (height 0) and an empty tree has height −1. Answering False usually comes from counting nodes instead of edges, which would make an empty tree height 0 and a single node height 1.
questions.page: On bst.html: press Clear to see Height = −1, then insert one value to see Height = 0.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, you insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60 in that order. List the keys visited by an In-Order traversal.
questions.hint: In-Order visits Left, then Root, then Right. What order does that always produce on a BST?
questions.explanation: In-Order (Left → Root → Right) visits every key smaller than a node before the node itself and every larger key after it, so on any valid BST it outputs the keys in strictly ascending sorted order: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. Answering "50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60" gives Level-Order (or insertion order here), while "50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60" is Pre-Order.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, choose In-Order, and press Traverse.

questions.prompt: A BST already contains 50, 30, and 70. What happens in this visualizer when you insert 30 again?
choices: The insertion is rejected because BST keys must be unique, and the tree is unchanged
30 is attached as the left child of the existing 30
30 is attached as the right child of the existing 30
The existing 30 is replaced and the tree size increases by 1
questions.answer: The insertion is rejected because BST keys must be unique, and the tree is unchanged
questions.explanation: This BST enforces strict inequalities (left < node < right) and unique keys: insert(30) walks from 50 to 30, flags a duplicate step, and leaves the tree and its size unchanged. Attaching duplicates to the left or right is a common guess from multiset BST variants, which this implementation explicitly rejects.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 50, 30, 70, type 30 into Value, and press Insert.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of searching for a key in a balanced Binary Search Tree with n nodes?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST, height h is approximately log₂ n and each comparison discards roughly half of the remaining nodes, so search follows one root-to-leaf path in O(log n) time. O(n) is tempting because it is the worst case for a skewed BST, while O(1) applies only to direct indexing or an average hash table lookup.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, you insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in that order. List the keys visited by a Pre-Order traversal.
questions.hint: Pre-Order visits the Root first, then finishes the entire Left subtree before touching the Right subtree.
questions.explanation: Pre-Order (Root → Left → Right) visits 50, then recursively traverses its entire left subtree (30, 20, 40), and only then traverses its right subtree (70, 60, 80). The most tempting wrong answer is "50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80", which is Level-Order (BFS) and jumps across to 70 before descending under 30.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, choose Pre-Order, and press Traverse.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, you insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 65 in that order (the default tree on bst.html), then delete 50. Which key becomes the new root?
questions.hint: 50 has two children. This BST replaces a two-child node with its in-order successor (the minimum key in its right subtree).
questions.explanation: 50 has two children (30 and 70), so delete(50) finds the in-order successor by stepping into the right subtree (70) and going left to 60. Copying 60 into the root and relinking 60's right child (65) under 70 preserves BST order. Answering 40 uses the in-order predecessor instead of the successor, and answering 70 promotes the immediate right child without finding the subtree minimum.
questions.page: On bst.html: keep the default list 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 65, type 50, and press Delete.

questions.prompt: In this BST visualizer, which statements about delete(key) are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Deleting a leaf node unlinks it from its parent without moving any other keys
Deleting a node with exactly one child promotes that child into the deleted node's place
Deleting a node with two children replaces its value with the in-order successor (minimum of its right subtree)
Deleting a node with two children always replaces its value with its immediate left child
answer: Deleting a leaf node unlinks it from its parent without moving any other keys
Deleting a node with exactly one child promotes that child into the deleted node's place
Deleting a node with two children replaces its value with the in-order successor (minimum of its right subtree)
questions.explanation: BST deletion handles three cases: a leaf is simply unlinked, a one-child node is bypassed by promoting its sole child, and a two-child node copies the value of its in-order successor (the leftmost node of its right subtree) and relinks the successor's right child. Promoting the immediate left child fails whenever that left child has a right subtree of its own, which would break the BST ordering invariant.
questions.page: On bst.html: test deleting a leaf (20), a one-child node (60), and a two-child node (50) on the default tree.

questions.prompt: You insert the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 in ascending sorted order into an empty Binary Search Tree. What is the worst-case time complexity of search, insert, or delete in such a skewed BST of n nodes?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
questions.explanation: Inserting keys in sorted order attaches every new key as a right child, creating a right-skewed chain of height h = n − 1 where searching for the deepest key or a missing larger key checks all n nodes in O(n) time. O(log n) is the tempting wrong answer because people assume every BST stays balanced, but an unbalanced plain BST does not rotate.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, observe Height = 5, then search for 60.

questions.prompt: In this BST visualizer, negative integers (down to -99) and 0 are valid keys, and the tree holds up to 31 unique keys.
questions.explanation: BinarySearchTree allows any unique integer key (including 0 and negatives) with a capacity of 1 to 31, and bst.html accepts whole numbers from −99 to 999. Answering False is a common mistake from assuming tree keys must be positive numbers like sizes or 1-based labels.
questions.page: On bst.html: build -99, 0, 999 and check Size (3 / 31), Min (−99), and Max (999).

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, you insert 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50 in that order. List the keys visited by a Post-Order traversal.
questions.hint: Post-Order visits Left subtree, then Right subtree, and visits the Root very last.
questions.explanation: In this tree, 20 has children 10 and 30, and 60 has left child 50. Post-Order (Left → Right → Root) finishes the left subtree (10, 30, 20), then finishes the right subtree (50, 60), and visits root 40 last: 10, 30, 20, 50, 60, 40. Answering "10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60" gives In-Order instead, while putting 60 before 50 forgets that children come before their parent.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, choose Post-Order, and press Traverse.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, you insert 40, 20, 60, 50, 70, 55 in that order, then delete 40. List the remaining keys in Level-Order (breadth-first, top to bottom and left to right).
questions.hint: Find 40's in-order successor (50). After copying 50 to the root, where does 50's right child 55 attach?
questions.explanation: Deleting two-child root 40 copies its in-order successor 50 into the root and relinks 50's right child (55) as the new left child of 60. Level 0 is 50, level 1 is 20 and 60, and level 2 is 55 and 70, so Level-Order visits 50, 20, 60, 55, 70. Answering "50, 20, 60, 70, 55" puts 55 on the wrong side of 60, and answering "50, 20, 60, 70" forgets to relink the successor's right child 55.
questions.page: On bst.html: build 40, 20, 60, 50, 70, 55, delete 40, then run Level-Order traversal.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of any full tree traversal (In-Order, Pre-Order, Post-Order, or Level-Order) on a Binary Search Tree with n nodes?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Every full traversal visits each of the n nodes and crosses each of the n − 1 edges a constant number of times, so all four traversals run in O(n) time regardless of whether the tree is balanced or skewed. O(n log n) is tempting because In-Order yields sorted keys, but the tree is already ordered by construction, so reading it out takes linear time.

questions.prompt: Which statements are guaranteed to hold for ANY valid non-empty Binary Search Tree of n unique keys (as in this visualizer)? Select all that apply.
choices: In-Order traversal visits all keys in strictly ascending order
The minimum key is found by following left pointers from the root until left is null
The in-order successor of a node with two children never has a left child
The tree height is always O(log n)
Level-Order traversal always visits keys in sorted order
answer: In-Order traversal visits all keys in strictly ascending order
The minimum key is found by following left pointers from the root until left is null
The in-order successor of a node with two children never has a left child
questions.explanation: Because left < node < right holds recursively, In-Order is always strictly ascending, the leftmost node from the root is always the minimum, and the minimum of a node's right subtree (its in-order successor) cannot have a left child—if it did, that left child would be an even smaller key in the right subtree. Height is NOT guaranteed to be O(log n) in an unbalanced BST (sorted input gives height n − 1), and Level-Order visits by depth, not sorted value.
